title: Three perfect days in Miami: polo on the sand, a lighthouse and the Book Fair
dek: Free beach polo behind the Setai, a ranger-led climb up Miami's oldest structure on Key Biscayne, two Heat home games and the opening day of the 43rd Miami Book Fair downtown.

hero.caption: The Cape Florida Lighthouse at the southern tip of Key Biscayne, in Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park.

intro:
Mid-November is when Miami is at its easiest: the heat has broken, the water is still warm, and the big December art crowds are three weeks away. This weekend the city has put a lot of its calendar on the water and the sand.

From Thursday to Sunday the **Miami Beach Polo World Cup** is played on the beach between 21st and 22nd streets, behind the Setai, and watching from the barrier around the field is free. Out on Biscayne Bay, the all-electric **E1** powerboat series holds its season finale, a doubleheader off Watson Island on Friday and Saturday. On Saturday the U.S. men's national team plays Haiti in a Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal at Nu Stadium, a match moved to Miami because of the security situation in Haiti, and the Heat are home on both Friday and Saturday nights.

Then on Sunday the **Miami Book Fair** opens its 43rd edition at Miami Dade College's Wolfson Campus downtown, with a free "Made in Miami" street party featuring Oscar G and Ciro Llerena, and the first night of its *Evenings With* series.

The plan follows that calendar. Friday is South Beach on foot: the south tip of the island, polo on the sand, design history at the Wolfsonian (free on Friday nights) and tapas on Española Way. Saturday crosses the Rickenbacker Causeway to Key Biscayne for the lighthouse, a beach and a sunset drink on Virginia Key, then back downtown for the Heat. Sunday is brunch and contemporary art in the Design District before the Book Fair opens, and dinner in the Upper Eastside.

days.title: Friday: South Beach on foot
days.intro: Everything today is within a few blocks of Washington Avenue and Collins, from the southern tip of the island up to the polo field at 21st Street.

stops.name: La Sandwicherie
stops.text: A South Beach counter that has fed the neighborhood at all hours for decades. Breakfast sandwiches on toasted croissant or baguette are served from 7 to 11 a.m., and every sandwich comes with the house French vinaigrette, which it also sells by the bottle. Order a croissant breakfast sandwich and eat it at the counter, then walk south. It is open every day from 7 a.m. to 5 a.m., so it is also the answer to a very late night.

stops.name: South Pointe Park
stops.text: The southern tip of Miami Beach, where Government Cut meets the ocean. Walk the shaded paths and the waterfront promenade, then go out on the pier to watch cruise ships and freighters slide through the channel to PortMiami, close enough to read their names. On a November morning the light is soft and the beach to the north is still quiet. There are restrooms, benches and a small playground; bring water and sunscreen, because the shade runs out on the pier.

stops.name: Miami Beach Polo World Cup
stops.addr: Beach behind the Setai, 2201 Collins Ave
stops.text: Polo on sand, played on a field built on the beach between 21st and 22nd streets. Friday's matches are scheduled at 1, 2:15, 3:30 and 4:45 p.m., and you can watch for free from the padded barrier around the field. For shade and a seat, the Don Julio Polo Lounge was listed from about $88 a day. Sit through at least two chukkers: the ponies tire quickly in sand, so the changes come fast. Check the event site for any schedule change before you go.

stops.name: The Wolfsonian–FIU
stops.text: Mitchell Wolfson Jr.'s collection of design and propaganda from 1850 to 1950, in a 1927 Mediterranean Revival storage building at 10th and Washington: posters, furniture, industrial design and decorative arts that explain how the modern world was sold to people. It is the best indoor companion to the Art Deco streets outside. Admission is free on Fridays from 6 to 9 p.m. (normally $12 for adults, and free for Florida residents and veterans). Closed Monday and Tuesday.

stops.name: Tropezón
stops.text: An Andalusian tapas bar on the pink Mediterranean-revival block of Española Way, from the team behind Lost Boy. Share tortilla española, patatas bravas and the boquerones fritos, then the roasted suckling pig if there are three or more of you. The gin list is the point at the bar: Negronis and gin-and-tonics. It opens at 4 p.m. and serves until 2 a.m. on Fridays; book for 8 p.m. or later, when it is loudest.

stops.name: Mac's Club Deuce
stops.text: Opened in 1926 and 100 years old this year, the Deuce is one of Miami Beach's oldest bars: neon, a pool table, a jukebox and bartenders who have seen everything. Anthony Bourdain called it one of his favorite places. Nothing about it has been modernized, which is why people keep coming. Bring patience at the bar on a Friday, and walk back across 14th Street to La Sandwicherie if you need a sandwich at 2 a.m.

days.title: Saturday: Key Biscayne and a Heat night
days.intro: Cross the Rickenbacker Causeway early for the lighthouse and the beach, take the sunset on Virginia Key, then come back downtown for dinner and the Heat.

stops.name: Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park
stops.text: The southern end of Key Biscayne: a mile of beach, sea grape and trails, with the Miami skyline across the water. The park opens at 8 a.m. and costs $8 a car; on busy weekends it closes for at least two hours once it is full, so arrive by 9. Walk the beach toward the lighthouse first, before the sun is high. Shoes and water help on the trails; the fishing piers are closed for repairs.
stops.wiki: Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park

stops.name: Cape Florida Lighthouse
stops.text: The brick lighthouse at the tip of the island was first lit in 1825, burned in an 1836 attack during the Second Seminole War and was rebuilt; it is among the oldest structures in the Miami area. Ranger-led tours run at 10 a.m. and 1 p.m., Thursday to Monday, with no extra fee or reservation; the tower and keeper's cottage are open only during tours. Climb the 109 spiral steps for a view over Stiltsville and the reef line. Get to the base a few minutes early.

stops.name: Boater's Grill
stops.text: An open-air restaurant inside the park on No Name Harbor, where sailboats anchor in a mangrove-lined basin. The menu runs from burgers to seafood, with paella and Florida lobster; the Florida Rambler recommends the Cuban fried pork chunks and the grilled snapper. Shoes and shirts are required, and there is a small air-conditioned room if the midday sun is too much. Stay for a walk around the harbor after lunch.

stops.name: Crandon Park
stops.text: Head back up the island for the afternoon on Crandon's wide beach, where the water stays shallow and calm and there is a fossilized reef and mangrove wetlands to explore. Walk to the Marjory Stoneman Douglas Biscayne Nature Center if you want to learn what you are wading through. Parking is $10 on weekends. Leave by about 4:45 to catch the sunset on Virginia Key.

stops.name: Rusty Pelican
stops.text: A waterfront restaurant on Virginia Key that looks straight back across the bay at the Brickell skyline, which is why you come at sunset rather than for a full meal. Take a cocktail on the terrace and watch the towers light up as the sun drops, a little before 5:40 p.m. this time of year. Then it is about 15 minutes over the causeway to downtown. Booking a terrace table is wise on a Saturday.

stops.name: ViceVersa
stops.text: An Italian cocktail bar and pizzeria on the ground floor of the Elser Hotel, a short walk from the arena, from the team behind Jaguar Sun. Start with the scallop crudo in tomato water, then a neo-Neapolitan pie such as The Italian Job, with vodka sauce, sausage and 'nduja. Leave room for the Affogato Martini. It is the right size for a dinner before an 8 p.m. tipoff; arrive by 6:30 to finish in time.

stops.name: Heat vs. Pistons at Kaseya Center
stops.text: The Heat host the Detroit Pistons at 8 p.m. in the bayfront arena, their second home game in two nights. Miami crowds arrive late and get loud in the fourth quarter. The arena is on the Metromover's Omni Loop (Freedom Tower and Park West stations are closest), which saves you the parking. Buy through the Heat's official ticketing to avoid resale markups.

days.title: Sunday: the Design District and the Book Fair
days.intro: Brunch and free contemporary art in the Design District, then downtown for the Book Fair's opening day, and dinner a few miles up Biscayne Boulevard.

stops.name: Michael's Genuine Food & Drink
stops.text: Michael Schwartz's bistro opened in 2007 and is still the Design District's neighborhood restaurant, with a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a menu that changes with what is local. Sunday brunch runs from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.; sit in the courtyard under the fans and order something from the wood oven and a plate of house-cured meats to share. Reservations are taken on OpenTable and Resy, and a Sunday booking is a good idea.

stops.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami
stops.text: A free museum of contemporary art in a three-story building with a sculpture garden, a block from brunch. It shows living and recently active artists, often in their first U.S. museum exhibitions, so you see work before it is everywhere. Galleries are open Wednesday to Sunday, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and there is a free tour of the current exhibitions daily at noon. Admission is free, but book a timed ticket online for guaranteed entry.

stops.name: Miami Design District
stops.text: Luxury shops, galleries and public art laid out over a former furniture district. Walk Palm Court to see Buckminster Fuller's Fly's Eye Dome, then wander the passages between NE 38th and 41st streets, where the architecture of the stores is half the show. If you are not shopping, the public art and the shade make it a good hour's walk. Check individual store hours on the district's site, as Sunday hours vary.

stops.name: Miami Book Fair: opening day
stops.addr: Miami Dade College Wolfson Campus, 300 NE 2nd Ave
stops.text: The 43rd Miami Book Fair opens today, with nearly 500 authors over eight days. Sunday brings a free "Made in Miami" party celebrating South Florida's music history, with Oscar G and Ciro Llerena, and the first night of *Evenings With*: five conversations, three of them free, including Tony Shalhoub with Josie Adams on their book about food and family. Times had not been posted widely when we wrote, so check the fair guide and reserve the ticketed talks early.

stops.name: Double Luck
stops.text: A Chinese-American restaurant from the founders of Tâm Tâm, chef Tam Pham and sommelier Harrison Ramhofer, that started as a pop-up and now has a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Order the crab rangoon (a whole crab claw in wonton), the tempura eggplant in fish-fragrant sauce and the Hennessy orange chicken, flambéed at the table. Its listed price range is $16 to $30. Book on Resy and confirm Sunday hours, which can change.

stay.name: The Ritz-Carlton Key Biscayne, Miami
stay.text: An oceanfront resort on Key Biscayne that reopened this spring after a $100 million renovation, with new rooms, a wellness wing, Luma for Italian and the open-air Aegean restaurant Paralía. It puts you minutes from the lighthouse and Crandon Park for Saturday, away from the noise of South Beach, with a causeway drive to everything else.

stay.name: Fontainebleau Miami Beach
stay.text: Morris Lapidus's 1954 curve on Collins Avenue, the hotel that set the style for Miami Beach glamour, on 20 oceanfront acres. The last phase of a multi-year renovation finished this year with a redone Versailles Tower. It is a straight run down Collins to the polo on Friday, and big enough that you never have to leave if you don't want to.

stay.name: Kasa El Paseo Miami Beach
stay.text: A Mediterranean-style hotel on Española Way with digital check-in and beach chairs and towels included, plus an hour's e-bike rental. It is steps from Tropezón, a short walk to the Wolfsonian and the polo field, and a sensible base for a Friday spent entirely on foot.

events.name: Miami Beach Polo World Cup
events.when: Thu. to Sun., Nov. 12 to 15; Fri. matches from 1 p.m., Sat. from noon, Sun. from 12:30 p.m.
events.where: On the beach behind the Setai, 2201 Collins Ave, Miami Beach
events.text: Four days of beach polo between 21st and 22nd streets. Watching from the barrier around the field is free; lounge and VIP tickets are sold separately. Saturday includes a celebrity match at 2 p.m.

events.name: E1 Miami GP
events.when: Fri. and Sat.; group stages from 10:30 a.m., Race Off at noon
events.where: Miami Seaplane Base, 1000 MacArthur Causeway, Watson Island
events.text: The season finale of the UIM E1 World Championship for all-electric hydrofoil powerboats, a doubleheader on Biscayne Bay, with teams owned by Tom Brady and Will Smith among them. Trackside access is through hospitality packages.

events.name: Miami Heat vs. Cleveland Cavaliers
events.text: The first of two Heat home games this weekend.

events.name: USMNT vs. Haiti, Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal
events.where: Nu Stadium, near Miami International Airport
events.text: The first leg of the quarterfinal, moved from Kingston to Miami because of the security situation in Haiti. The second leg is in Cincinnati on Tuesday.

events.name: Miami Heat vs. Detroit Pistons
events.text: The Heat's second home game in two nights.

events.name: Miami Book Fair opening day
events.when: Sun.; the fair runs Nov. 15 to 22, with the Street Fair Nov. 20 to 22
events.where: Miami Dade College Wolfson Campus, downtown
events.text: The 43rd fair opens with a free "Made in Miami" party featuring Oscar G and Ciro Llerena, and the first night of the Evenings With series, including Tony Shalhoub and Josie Adams.

know: From Miami International (MIA), take the free MIA Mover to the Miami Intermodal Center and Metrorail downtown, about 25 to 30 minutes. A taxi or ride-hail to South Beach takes 25 to 40 minutes. Fort Lauderdale (FLL) is the other airport, farther north.

The Metromover is free and loops through downtown and Brickell, stopping near Kaseya Center and the Book Fair. Metrorail and Metrobus cost about $2.25 a ride. For Key Biscayne you need a car or ride-hail: the Rickenbacker Causeway toll is $1.75 leaving Miami, and Bill Baggs charges $8 a car.

Saturday afternoon is busy on the roads: the USMNT plays Haiti at 4:30 p.m. at Nu Stadium next to the airport, the Hurricanes host Duke at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, and the Heat tip off downtown at 8 p.m. Leave extra time for any airport run.

The E1 powerboat races on Friday and Saturday are staged at the Miami Seaplane Base on the MacArthur Causeway, and parking there is limited; expect slow traffic between downtown and South Beach on race mornings.
Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park closes for at least two hours once it is full on weekends. Arrive by 9 a.m. on Saturday. The lighthouse is open only during the 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. tours.
Sunset is a little before 5:40 p.m. Plan the beach for midday and the Wolfsonian for Friday evening, when it is free from 6 to 9 p.m.
Many Miami restaurants add a service charge to the bill, so check before tipping. Where none is added, 18 to 20 percent is usual.
Veterans Day is Wednesday, November 11. The Wolfsonian admits veterans and active military free with ID.
